No line-by-line technical description was included beyond the title, so the prompt below converts the publicly documented structure and mechanics into a debranded, single build specification that preserves the core feature set while omitting the original title inside the prompt.[1][2][3][4][5]

## Prompt

Build a full, production-ready, open-world action-adventure game set on a vast alien frontier with dense forests, sweeping plains, floating or towering landforms, hazardous industrial zones, and a living ecosystem that reacts to player presence, resource gathering, wildlife disruption, and hostile occupation. The game must center on an indigenous protagonist who was abducted as a child by a human extraction-and-military corporation, trained to serve that corporation, placed into long-term suspended stasis, and later awakened as a stranger in their own homeland; the main narrative arc must follow their return to their culture, reconnection with their heritage, alliance-building with multiple local clans, and organized resistance against renewed colonization across a large frontier divided into three distinct major regions with unique biomes, traversal problems, fauna, weather, visual identity, and quest logic.[2][3][4][1]

Construct the entire software stack from scratch and deliver complete, unabridged, production-ready source code for all runtime systems, tools, data definitions, shaders, UI, networking, save/load, build scripts, editor utilities, automated tests, and technical documentation. Do not output summaries, stubs, placeholders, fake integrations, mocked assets, dummy functions, pseudocode, or “to be implemented later” sections. Do not mention the commercial title anywhere in the prompt output, code, filenames, menus, comments, documentation, metadata, or user-facing text. Create original production assets and data that match the required functional scope without copying protected names, logos, dialogue, cinematics, map layouts, or art assets.

Begin by defining the project architecture. Use a modern real-time 3D engine and organize the codebase into clear modules for engine bootstrap, rendering, world partition and streaming, terrain and foliage, physics, animation, camera, input, audio, AI, quest logic, dialogue, cinematics, combat, stealth, vehicles and mounts, crafting, inventory, progression, UI, save systems, multiplayer synchronization, telemetry, performance profiling, and platform abstraction. Establish a deterministic data-driven framework so quests, enemies, wildlife, weapons, recipes, traversal objects, world events, biomes, and faction rules are authored in external data files and loaded by validated runtime schemas. Build continuous integration, asset validation, automated gameplay smoke tests, performance regression tests, and crash logging from the start.

Then implement the world. Create three large open regions with seamless traversal, streaming cells, biome-specific lighting, weather, ambient audio, vegetation sets, wildlife populations, traversal affordances, and enemy occupation patterns.  The world must feel alive and reactive rather than static, with systemic interactions between flora, fauna, industrial contamination, combat damage, weather, fire, stealth cover, and harvesting systems.  Implement day-night cycles, volumetric atmosphere, long-range visibility, dense ecosystem simulation, navigable verticality, hidden routes, climbable surfaces, glide and leap opportunities, and discoverable side content that rewards exploration without reducing the world to repetitive map icons.[1][2]

Next, build the player controller and traversal stack. Support a primary first-person mode and an optional seamless third-person mode, with complete animation, camera collision, aiming, parkour, and locomotion support for both.  Implement high-agility movement with sprinting, sliding, mantling, ledge grabbing, climbing, wall-adjacent movement, long jumping, rapid directional changes, aerial recovery, and a double-jump-like traversal extension that preserves the fantasy of superior physical mobility.  Make traversal one of the core pleasures of the game by tuning acceleration, landing, inertia, camera motion, field-of-view changes, footstep response, and environmental interaction so moving through forests, cliffs, ruins, and industrial facilities is fluid and readable.[3][4][5][6][2]

After that, implement perception, survival, and progression. Add an enhanced sensory mode that highlights interactable plants, harvestable materials, enemy weak points, tracks, environmental clues, mission objectives, and systemic world states without cluttering the screen.  Build health, stamina, status effects, nutrition or temporary buff systems, skill trees, equipment slots, stat modifiers, and layered progression driven by exploration, quest completion, clan reputation, crafting quality, and combat mastery. Add contextual tutorials, codex discovery, bestiary and flora databases, and elegant onboarding that teaches systems through play rather than intrusive interruption.[2]

Then build combat. Support both indigenous weapons and human-made firearms, with distinct handling models, animation sets, sound signatures, ammo rules, upgrade paths, and tactical roles.  Implement bows, heavy bows, thrown spears, close-range tools, assault firearms, shotguns, explosives, traps, stealth takedowns, environmental kills, enemy armor states, vulnerable components, weak-point damage, stagger, suppression, and destructible industrial machinery.  Make encounters work for stealth, mobility, precision, or aggressive playstyles, and ensure combat AI can search, flank, call reinforcements, patrol, investigate sound, defend facilities, use elevation, and react to wildlife interference.[2]

Build gathering, hunting, and crafting as full systemic loops rather than menu abstractions. Let players collect natural materials, process components, cook or prepare consumables, and craft gear, ammunition, throwables, upgrades, and specialized tools.  Implement material rarity, quality tiers, biome dependencies, weather-sensitive harvesting windows, and recipe trees. Preserve a rule where using firearms on animals damages or invalidates resource collection, forcing the player to think about hunting method and ecosystem respect.  Tie crafted quality to harvesting precision, timing, tool selection, and character skills.[2]

Implement a personal flying mount as a major traversal and combat system. The player must be able to bond with a unique aerial creature, summon it, take off and land dynamically, navigate at high speed over large distances, engage in aerial pursuit and aerial combat, and use it as both transportation and identity expression.  Build flight physics, stamina, collision avoidance, altitude rules, aerial enemy behaviors, mounted attacks, upgrade paths, animations, call-and-response audio, and mission scripting that uses the mount for traversal, escape, scouting, combat, and cinematic travel.[3]

Construct the narrative and quest framework next. Build a full campaign that starts with captivity aftermath and cultural dislocation, expands into exploration and trust-building, then escalates into regional liberation, sabotage of extractive infrastructure, clan unification, and a final large-scale confrontation.  Support main quests, side quests, clan quests, exploration discoveries, world events, faction encounters, environmental storytelling, dialogue trees where appropriate, scripted set pieces, and branching state changes that reflect player action. Include a reputation or favor economy in which helping clans, defeating occupying forces, and progressing key storylines unlock rare gear, resources, and narrative access.[4][1][3][2]

Build full AI ecosystems. Wildlife must have species-specific schedules, sensory models, flocking or pack logic, feeding, territoriality, fear, predation, and reactions to player noise, weather, gunfire, fire, and industrial activity. Human enemies must operate bases, convoys, patrol routes, alarm networks, scanners, vehicles, and extraction sites, with layered alert states and recoverable world-state behaviors. The game should support emergent interactions in which wildlife, stealth, explosives, environmental hazards, and enemy faction behavior intersect naturally.

Add optional two-player online cooperative play as a first-class system, not a bolt-on mode. Support drop-in/drop-out play, synchronized world state, mission progression rules, replicated traversal, mounted travel, combat, crafting, loot distribution, revive states, checkpointing, join permissions, and difficulty scaling for cooperative sessions.  Ensure the game remains fully playable in single-player and that co-op integration does not break quest logic, cinematic sequencing, AI behavior, or save integrity.[4][2]

Build a complete interface and user-experience layer. Include controller, keyboard, and mouse support; remapping; accessibility settings; subtitle and caption systems; difficulty presets and granular assists; aim, motion, and camera settings; color-blind-safe UI; readable HUD customization; objective tracking; map and compass systems; codex navigation; inventory and crafting screens; quest journals; mount management; photo mode; and save-slot management. Keep navigation readable and immersive, favoring diegetic cues, environmental guidance, and clean presentation over excessive icon spam.

Complete the audiovisual layer at production quality. Implement high-density ambient soundscapes, biome-specific music states, stealth and combat transitions, wildlife spatial audio, industrial sound signatures, mount vocalizations, reactive score cues, and cinematic mixing. Build physically based materials, foliage wind response, atmospheric scattering, volumetrics, wetness, particle systems, destruction effects, shader-driven alien bioluminescence, weather transitions, and day-night lighting coherence. Use scalable quality tiers so the game can target stable performance on modern hardware while preserving high-end visual fidelity.

Finish with shipping requirements. Deliver a runnable game with all files present, full source code, content pipelines, build instructions, technical documentation, editor tooling, automated tests, profiling notes, and release configuration. Verify stability, memory budgets, loading times, streaming performance, animation correctness, input latency, network resilience, quest completion integrity, save/load safety, and platform compliance. The final output must be complete software, not a design pitch, and every subsystem required to play the full game from start to finish must be implemented in production-ready form.

**Avatar: Frontiers of Pandora** should be rewritten as a single technical prompt that instructs a model to build a complete, production-ready open-world action game system from scratch, with all files included and no placeholders, while avoiding any mention of the original software name in the prompt itself. The prompt should explicitly require a fully working, unabridged implementation with complete source code, assets, UI, game loop, input, rendering, audio, saving, and testing hooks, and it should be framed as a build specification rather than a request for commentary or roleplay .

## Prompt structure

Start by defining the target as a full browser game or game system, then specify the required technical stack, architecture, and delivery format. The prompt should state that the implementation must be production-ready, complete across all files, and written as if the system is being built from the ground up, with step-by-step construction from core architecture through gameplay, rendering, UI, and validation .

## Required build scope

The prompt should require a real game foundation with a fixed-timestep game loop, WebGL 2 rendering, physics, asset loading from CDNs when needed, responsive UI, accessibility-aware overlays, and proper state management. It should also require real art direction, distinct visual identity, and complete screens such as title, loading, pause, game-over, and settings, all implemented as functional software rather than simulated content .

## Delivery constraints

The prompt should insist on complete, unabridged, production-ready code for every file, with no simplified, mock, dummy, fake, or placeholder content. It should also forbid naming or referencing the original software title inside the prompt, while still demanding that the resulting system faithfully capture the same genre, scale, and gameplay intent through original implementation details .

Here is the single comprehensive prompt:

```text
Build a complete, production-ready open-world action game system from scratch as a fully functional static browser application. Construct every file required for the project and provide complete, unabridged source code only. Do not include simplified, mock, dummy, simulated, placeholder, or fake content. Do not omit any subsystem, asset pipeline step, or runtime file necessary for the game to run end to end.

Begin by establishing the full project architecture. Use a single HTML entry point with embedded or linked CSS and JavaScript, organized into clearly separated modules or sections for initialization, rendering, asset loading, input handling, audio, world simulation, user interface, save/load state, debugging, and cleanup. Create a complete game loop based on time step logic rather than frame-dependent logic. Ensure the loop supports deterministic update steps, smooth rendering, and stable performance at variable frame rates.

Build the game world as a fully explorable 3D environment with streaming or staged world loading, environmental variety, interactive terrain, traversal systems, AI-controlled characters, mission or objective logic, combat or interaction systems, and progression mechanics. Implement the player controller, camera system, movement physics, collision handling, interaction detection, enemy behavior, world events, and game state transitions in a way that works in real gameplay, not as scripted demonstration content.

Implement the visual system with a coherent high-fidelity art direction. Include complete scene lighting, atmospheric effects, terrain materials, foliage, water or reflective surfaces where appropriate, sky rendering, post-processing, UI overlays, and polished transitions between states. Use original assets or verified external assets only; every image, model, texture, sound, and font must be real and must be integrated into the application with correct loading, dimensions, and fallback behavior. Do not use placeholder art or empty boxes.

Build all screens and overlays required for a finished game: title screen, loading screen, main menu, pause menu, settings, objective HUD, inventory or equipment interface if needed, dialogue or tutorial overlays, fail states, and completion states. All interface elements must be functional, keyboard-accessible where appropriate, visually coherent, and responsive across desktop and mobile layouts. Include proper labels, focus states, and error handling.

Implement real audio systems, including background music, ambient sound, sound effects, and state-based audio transitions. Ensure audio initialization respects browser interaction requirements and that all sounds are loaded from valid sources. Add controls for volume and audio toggles in settings.

Include save and restore functionality for persistent game progress only if it can be implemented without unsupported browser storage; otherwise, implement in-memory state and session-scoped logic that remains fully operational inside the browser sandbox. Do not rely on unavailable APIs. All game state, progress, mission tracking, and UI state must remain internally consistent.

Provide a complete debugging and validation layer. Add a visible debug overlay showing frame timing, FPS, draw calls or equivalent performance metrics, active entity counts, and current scene or mission state. Add testing hooks for deterministic simulation, input replay, and state inspection so the system can be evaluated reliably. Include proper cleanup for event listeners, animation frames, audio resources, and GPU resources.

Use modern browser-compatible technology only. Use production-grade JavaScript, semantic HTML, and maintainable CSS. Prefer WebGL 2 for rendering. If physics is required, implement it with a browser-compatible physics engine that loads correctly in a sandboxed iframe. If models or textures must be loaded, use only CDN-hosted or otherwise verifiable URLs that work in the browser environment. Avoid any API known to be blocked in sandboxed iframes.

Structure the code as a complete game, not a prototype. Every subsystem must be integrated and functional. Every control must respond correctly. Every state must transition correctly. Every visual element must be intentionally designed. Every asset must load and display correctly. Every file required for the game must be included in full. Output only the final implementation, with no explanations, no summaries, and no placeholders.
```

```text
Build a coherent AI architecture for hostile enemies, wildlife, and neutral world actors. Wildlife must roam, flee, herd or pack where appropriate, react to weather, combat, and nearby actors, and contribute to the feeling of a living frontier. AI state must be data-driven, debuggable, and observable through development overlays.

Create a mission and progression framework that supports a full campaign structure, side activities, dynamic objectives, unlocks, and stateful world progression. The narrative structure should center on an indigenous protagonist reclaiming identity after forced separation by a militarized extraction force, rebuilding connection to homeland and allied clans, and resisting industrial occupation across multiple regions. Implement mission state machines, objective tracking, triggers, fail and success conditions, scripted moments, exploration-driven discoveries, and state transitions that affect world conditions, enemy presence, unlocked traversal routes, and available gear or abilities. This must function as a real gameplay campaign framework, not a sequence of disconnected demos.

Implement layered combat with multiple distinct styles. Support precision traditional ranged weapons, thrown weapons, melee or close-range interactions where appropriate, and heavier industrial firearms with different handling, recoil, damage profiles, and resource costs. Include aiming, projectile simulation or hitscan where appropriate, enemy weak points, health and damage systems, stagger or stun behavior, stealth takedowns or silent approaches, destructible interactables, alarm systems, and contextual environmental combat opportunities. Combat must integrate with traversal, stealth, AI, and mission logic.

Build gathering, crafting, inventory, and equipment systems as real gameplay features. The player must be able to collect natural resources, salvage hostile technology or industrial materials, craft or upgrade gear, consume useful items, and equip different tools or weapons. Inventory data, item definitions, recipes, upgrade trees, resource qualities, and equipment stats must all be implemented as real game data with validation and serialization support. UI for these systems must be complete, navigable, and synchronized with game state.

Include a personal aerial mount or equivalent high-speed creature-based traversal system as a major gameplay pillar. Implement summoning rules, mounting and dismounting, flight controls, altitude handling, traversal acceleration, aerial camera behavior, collision safety, landing logic, traversal-specific stamina or cooldown balancing where needed, and integration with world streaming and combat. The mount must feel like an actual traversal layer that changes route planning, exploration speed, and combat possibilities rather than a cosmetic animation.

Build all required screens, overlays, and interface layers for a finished game. Include a title screen, boot or loading screen, main menu, settings menu, pause menu, HUD, objective tracker, interaction prompts, tutorial overlays, codex or journal view, inventory and equipment screens, map or navigation screen, fail state, completion state, and any dialogue or mission briefing surfaces required by the design. Every UI screen must be fully functional, visually coherent, responsive across desktop and mobile layouts, and accessible by keyboard where appropriate. Include focus states, labels, reduced-motion support, readable contrast, scalable text, and robust error handling for missing assets or unsupported interactions.

Implement a full audio stack. Include music playback, ambient loops, localized sound effects, UI sounds, combat audio, environmental audio zones, and dynamic transitions based on game state. Audio must initialize only after valid browser interaction when necessary. Provide full volume controls, mute toggles, category mixing, pause behavior, and cleanup. Every sound asset reference must be real, verified, and integrated correctly. Handle load failures gracefully without breaking the runtime.

Implement asset loading and validation for textures, models, audio, fonts, and data files. Use only verified external asset URLs or locally included assets that actually exist and load correctly in the browser environment. If CDN-hosted resources are used, they must be production-safe, publicly accessible, version-pinned where possible, and compatible with sandboxed browser execution. Add loading progress tracking, retry or fail reporting, fallback handling, and explicit error surfaces so asset problems are visible during development and recoverable at runtime where feasible.

Implement save and restore behavior in a way that remains valid inside a sandboxed browser environment. Do not depend on browser APIs that are unavailable or unreliable in sandboxed iframes. If durable persistence cannot be guaranteed in the runtime environment, implement an internal session-based save system with deterministic state snapshots, mission progress recovery during the active session, restart support, and developer-triggered export or import hooks that work within the available browser constraints. The save layer must keep world state, mission state, inventory, settings, and progression internally consistent.

Add a comprehensive debug and test layer. Include an in-game debug overlay that displays frame timing, FPS, update cost, render cost, entity counts, active region counts, mission state, camera mode, player coordinates, streaming status, and memory-sensitive metrics where measurable. Include deterministic stepping hooks, input recording and replay hooks, state inspection tools, seed-based world generation hooks, collision visualization toggles, AI debug views, and validation utilities for assets, missions, and serialization. The final codebase must be testable and diagnosable without modifying core logic.

Define a strong and original visual identity rather than relying on generic sci-fi defaults. Establish a clear color system, typography, UI styling, lighting language, atmospheric palette, and environmental art direction that supports a lush alien frontier, industrial intrusion, and cultural resistance. All visuals must be intentionally designed and implemented with real assets, real shaders, real layout decisions, and coherent state transitions. Do not use empty panels, gray boxes, or temporary art. The software must look and behave like a cohesive shipped product.

Ensure the final implementation is complete across all files: HTML, CSS, JavaScript modules, shaders, data files, asset manifests, configuration files, and any runtime support files needed for the browser build. The output must be a full project that can run end to end as a real browser game system. Every subsystem must be integrated. Every control must work. Every screen must function. Every transition must be real. Every asset reference must resolve. Every required file must be included in full. Output only the final project contents.
```

This version is stricter than the original because it explicitly encodes the source game’s documented pillars—open-world frontier exploration, dual-perspective action-adventure play, clan- and identity-driven resistance framing, crafting and multiple combat styles, personal aerial traversal, optional two-player co-op, and exploration-oriented presentation—without naming the original title inside the prompt body.[6][2][4][7][5][1]
